title: Ser and tener
topic: ser and tener in the present; definite and indefinite articles; gender and plural of nouns
why: Your very first Spanish lesson: we set up ser and tener, the articles and the plural, before any other verb. You'll use these two verbs from your first conversation to give your nationality, age and job, and they prepare the regular verbs of the next lesson.

{"lessons": ["

Ser and tener: the two pillars

Welcome to your first Spanish lesson! We start with the two most useful verbs: ser (to be) and tener (to have). Just like \"to be\" and \"to have\" in English, they're irregular: learn them by heart, out loud.

ser (to be)tener (to have)
yo (I)soytengo
tú (you, one friend)erestienes
él, ella, usted (he, she, you formal)estiene
nosotros, nosotras (we)somostenemos
vosotros, vosotras (you all, friends)soistenéis
ellos, ellas, ustedes (they, you all formal)sontienen

The subject is usually dropped: in English you always need \"I\" or \"you\", but in Spanish the verb ending already tells you who's speaking. You say Soy francés (I'm French); Yo soy francés is only for emphasis or contrast (Yo soy francés y tú eres español).

Soy francesa y tengo treinta años.I'm French (a woman speaking) and I'm thirty.

\"You\": tú, vosotros or usted?

English has a single \"you\". Spanish has four, depending on how many people you address and how formal you are. Besides the familiar form for one friend (in the table above), there are:

  • vosotros / vosotras = \"you\" for several people you're on first-name terms with (friends, colleagues): ¿Sois de Lyon?
  • usted = polite \"you\" for one person (think \"sir\" or \"ma'am\"). It takes the same verb form as él: ¿Usted es de Madrid? In the plural: ustedes, conjugated like ellos.

In Latin America, people don't use vosotros: they always say ustedes. In Spain, both are used.

Three structures to remember

  • Age uses tener, not \"to be\": Spanish literally says \"I have thirty years\": Tengo treinta años.
  • A job is given without an article, unlike English \"I'm a teacher\": Soy profesor (I'm a teacher), never \"soy un profesor\".
  • A yes/no question needs no \"do\" and no word swapping: intonation alone does it, and it's written between ¿ and ?: ¿Eres de París?

For ages, here are a few numbers until the lesson on numbers: uno (1), dos (2), tres (3), diez (10), veinte (20), treinta (30), cuarenta (40).

To say hi: ¡Hola! (hi, hello). To say \"nice to meet you\": encantado if you're a man, encantada if you're a woman.

", "

Articles and the gender of nouns

This is new for an English speaker: every Spanish noun is either masculine or feminine, even objects, and the article changes with the gender and the number. Where English has just \"the\" and \"a\", Spanish has eight forms.

definite (the)indefinite (a, some)
masculine singularel libroun libro
feminine singularla llaveuna llave
masculine plurallos librosunos libros
feminine plurallas llavesunas llaves

Two things to notice:

  • The gender also applies to people, of course: \"the friend\" is el amigo for a man, la amiga for a woman.
  • \"The\" has two plural forms: los (masculine) and las (feminine). Same for unos / unas (some, a few).

Recognizing the gender

  • Nouns ending in -o are almost always masculine: el libro, el amigo, el hermano.
  • Nouns ending in -a are almost always feminine: la amiga, la hermana, la casa.
  • Nouns ending in -dad and -ción are feminine: la ciudad, la estación.
  • For other endings, learn the noun with its article: el móvil, el ordenador, la llave, el coche.

A few exceptions to know right away: el día (the day), el mapa (the map), el idioma (the language) are masculine despite their -a.

Genders you can't guess

With endings like -e or a consonant, nothing tells you the gender: learn these with their article from day one.

SpanishEnglish
el cochethe car
el colorthe color
la lechethe milk
la salthe salt

Jobs and people often have two forms: el profesor / la profesora, el camarero / la camarera, el enfermero / la enfermera. Nouns ending in -ante don't change, only the article does: el estudiante / la estudiante.

Pablo tiene un ordenador y una llave.Pablo has a computer and a key.

Unlike English, nationalities are written with a lowercase letter, even for people: los franceses (the French). And watch the accent: francés has one, but francesa, franceses and francesas don't. Same for inglés → inglesa, alemán → alemana.

", "

The plural of nouns

Good news: the Spanish plural works a lot like the English one, with -s or -es.

The noun ends in…Examples
vowel → + -sel libro → los libros
la llave → las llaves
el coche → los coches
consonant → + -esel móvil → los móviles
la ciudad → las ciudades
el profesor → los profesores
-z → -cesel lápiz → los lápices

The written accent can move

When you add -es, the word gains a syllable, and the written accent appears or disappears so the stress stays in the same place:

  • el francés → los franceses, el alemán → los alemanes: the accent disappears.
  • el examen → los exámenes, el joven → los jóvenes: the accent appears.

Masculine plural for a mixed group

A group of men and women is referred to in the masculine plural. This gives Spanish handy words where English needs a different one:

SpanishMeaning
los hermanosthe brothers, or the siblings (brothers and sisters)
los amigosthe friends (men and women)
los padresthe parents (father and mother)

So to ask whether someone has any brothers or sisters, you simply say: ¿Tienes hermanos?

—¿Tienes hermanos? —Sí, tengo dos hermanos: un hermano y una hermana.—Do you have any siblings? —Yes, I have two: a brother and a sister.
Carmen y Javier son españoles. Son camareros.Carmen and Javier are Spanish. They're waiters.

The trap for an English speaker: since \"the\" never changes in English, you'll be tempted to use the same article everywhere. \"The keys\" is las llaves, not \"los llaves\". Always check the noun's gender in the singular: la llave → las llaves.
